title: Arrays, Strings, Functions & Recursion
intro: Arrays and matrices, strings and string functions, modular programming with functions, parameter passing and recursion.

sec.s: An array is a fixed-size collection of elements of the same type, stored in contiguous memory…

b.x: An array is a fixed-size collection of elements of the same type, stored in contiguous memory locations. Instead of declaring many unrelated variables such as mark1, mark2, mark3 and mark4, a program can declare one array called marks and access each element by an index. Arrays are central to processing lists, tables, strings, images, and many algorithmic data structures.
Example:

This declares an array capable of holding five int values. The valid indices are 0, 1, 2, 3, and 4. C uses zero-based indexing, so the first element is marks[0], not marks[1]. Accessing marks[5] is outside the array and causes undefined behavior. C does not automatically check array bounds at runtime.

Each element has the same declared element type. For int marks[5], every element is an int and occupies sizeof(int) bytes. The array’s elements are laid out consecutively in memory. The compiler may add padding inside structures, but ordinary array elements are contiguous with no gaps between successive elements beyond the size of each element.
Arrays are useful when:

x: Many values share the same type and purpose.
Data must be processed using loops.
A fixed-size table or buffer is appropriate.
Data must be passed to a function as a pointer to its first element.

b.x: An array is not the same as a linked list. Array indexing is constant-time when the index is valid, while a linked list normally requires traversal to reach an element by position. Arrays have a fixed size after declaration, except for dynamically allocated memory or variable-length arrays where supported. A dynamically allocated block can have a size chosen at runtime, but the programmer must manage its lifetime.

Use square brackets to access an element:

An array element behaves like an ordinary variable of the element type. It can be assigned, read, incremented, or used in an expression. The array name alone is not a single scalar element; in most expressions it is converted to a pointer to its first element. 2.5 Reversing an array
A common in-place algorithm swaps the first element with the last, the second with the second-last, and continues until the middle:

sec.s: A two-dimensional array can be understood as an array of arrays.

b.x: A two-dimensional array can be understood as an array of arrays. It is commonly used for matrices, grids, game boards, marks tables, and tabular data.
Declaration:

This means three rows, each containing four int elements. The first index selects the row and the second selects the column. Valid row indices are 0 through 2, and valid column indices are 0 through 3.
Initialization:
Access:
Nested loops are the normal way to traverse a 2D array:

The outer loop selects a row, and the inner loop visits every column in that row. Row-major storage means the elements of each row are contiguous, followed by the next row. For matrix[2][3], the logical order is: matrix[0][0], matrix[0][1], matrix[0][2], matrix[1][0], matrix[1][1], matrix[1][2].
3.1 Matrix addition
Two matrices can be added element by element when they have the same dimensions:
The result at each position is the sum of the corresponding input positions. This is an example of a nested loop whose body executes rows multiplied by columns times.
3.2 Matrix transpose
The transpose of a matrix exchanges rows and columns. For an m-by-n matrix, the transpose has n rows and m columns:

The destination must have dimensions suitable for the transposed result. For a square matrix, the same storage may be used with a carefully designed in-place algorithm, but the simple code above uses a separate array.
3.3 Passing a 2D array to a function
When passing a multidimensional array to a function, the function generally needs to know the size of all dimensions except the first, because it must calculate the offset for each row. For example:

x: void print_matrix(int rows, int cols, int a[rows][cols]) {

b.x: This uses a variable length array parameter form available in C99 and supported by many compilers. If a compiler or course uses a different C version, use a fixed column dimension or another representation and follow the compiler’s supported standard. A parameter written as int a[][4] still requires the column count to be known for addressing rows.

sec.s: Array elements occupy contiguous memory.

b.x: Array elements occupy contiguous memory. If an int occupies four bytes on a particular implementation, then adjacent int elements are typically four bytes apart. Do not hard-code that assumption: use sizeof(int) to obtain the size for the implementation.
For an actual array object, sizeof a gives the total byte size of the array, while sizeof a[0] gives the size of one element. Dividing the two gives the element count:

x: size_t count = sizeof a / sizeof a[0];

b.x: This technique works only while a is an actual array in that scope. When an array is passed to a function parameter, the parameter is adjusted to a pointer type, so sizeof the parameter reports the pointer size, not the original array size. Pass the element count separately.

Array indexing is closely related to pointer arithmetic. In most expressions, a[i] is equivalent to *(a + i). This does not mean the array itself is a pointer; the array expression is converted to a pointer to its first element in most contexts. The distinction matters for sizeof and the address-of operator.
Memory safety rules:

x: Never access an index outside 0 through length
Do not read uninitialized automatic array elements.
Do not return a pointer to a local array whose lifetime ends when the function returns.
Do not assume two arrays can be copied with assignment.
Ensure destination arrays are large enough for every write.
Use size_t for sizes and indexes when appropriate, but guard empty arrays carefully because size_t is unsigned.
Initialize data before using it and validate lengths received from input.

b.x: For a one-dimensional array, address offsets are based on the element size. If a points to a[0], then a + 1 points to a[1], not one byte after a[0]. Pointer arithmetic is scaled by the size of the pointed-to type. Valid pointer arithmetic is limited to elements of the same array object and one position past the end; dereferencing that one-past pointer is not allowed.

sec.s: C does not have a separate built-in string object type.

b.x: C does not have a separate built-in string object type. A C string is a sequence of char elements terminated by a null character, written ‘\0’. The null character has numeric value zero; it is not the same as the digit character ‘0’.
This creates an array containing six characters: ‘h’, ‘e’, ‘l’, ‘l’, ‘o’, and ‘\0’. The compiler adds the terminator when initializing an array from a string literal. The array can be modified:
After this change, it contains “Hello”.
A character array is not automatically a valid string. For example:

There is no room for a null terminator. It can be used as a three-character array, but passing it to a function expecting a C string may cause an out-of-bounds read. A string buffer needs space for the terminating ‘\0’.
A string literal such as “hello” has array type, but attempting to modify the literal through a pointer is undefined behavior. Prefer:
when a pointer refers to a string literal. Use a writable array if the characters must change.
5.1 Reading strings

scanf(“%s”, buffer) reads a sequence of non-whitespace characters and adds a terminating null character, but without a width limit it can overflow the buffer. For a buffer of 20 chars, a width of 19 reserves space for ‘\0’:
This does not read spaces in a full name. fgets is often preferable for a whole line:

fgets reads at most one less than the buffer capacity and terminates the string. It may keep a newline if one fits. If a line is longer than the buffer, the remainder remains in the input stream and may need additional handling. Input should always be bounded.
5.2 Character arrays versus strings

A char array stores characters, but only a sequence ending in ‘\0’ is a valid C string. The string-handling functions expect that terminator. They do not know the actual capacity of the array. This is why buffer capacity must be tracked separately and why functions such as strcpy and strcat can overflow when misused.

sec.s: The declarations for standard string functions are in <string.h>.

b.x: The declarations for standard string functions are in <string.h>. The main functions in this syllabus are strlen, strcpy, strcat, and strcmp. Each expects properly terminated strings, except that the destination capacity requirements differ by function.
6.1 strlen
strlen returns the number of characters before the terminating null character. The terminator is not included.

For char text[] = “hello”, strlen(text) is 5, while sizeof text is 6 because the array contains the terminator. This distinction is frequently tested in exams. strlen scans until it finds ‘\0’, so it is unsafe on a character array that lacks a terminator. Its return type is size_t, an unsigned type used for object sizes. Use %zu with printf to print a size_t value.
6.2 strcpy
strcpy copies a source string, including the terminating ‘\0’, into a destination array:

The destination must have enough space for every source character plus the terminator. strcpy does not know the destination’s capacity and does not perform bounds checking. If destination is too small, memory may be overwritten, causing undefined behavior and potentially a security defect. The source and destination should not overlap.

A safer design tracks the capacity explicitly and uses a suitable bounded copying strategy. strncpy is not a universal drop-in safe replacement because it may fail to terminate the destination when the source is too long. Always understand the exact behavior of the chosen function.
6.3 strcat
strcat appends the source string to the end of the destination string, overwriting the destination’s existing terminator and adding a new one.

first now contains “Good morning”. Its buffer must have room for the original destination length plus the source length plus one terminator. If the buffer is too small, strcat writes beyond its bounds. The source and destination must not overlap. Before concatenation, calculate the required capacity or use a design that maintains a known maximum length.
6.4 strcmp
strcmp compares two null-terminated strings lexicographically according to the character values used by the implementation. It returns:

x: A value less than zero if the first string compares less than the second.
Zero if the strings are equal.
A value greater than zero if the first string compares greater than the second.

b.x: Do not assume the result must be exactly -1 or 1. Test its sign:
C does not compare string contents using ==. For char arrays, == compares pointer-like expressions after array conversion, not every character. Use strcmp for content comparison.
6.5 Example using the four functions

The example uses buffers large enough for the expected text. In larger programs, capacities should be calculated or checked rather than guessed. Never pass untrusted text into an unbounded copy or append operation.

sec.s: A function is a named unit of code that performs a task.

b.x: A function is a named unit of code that performs a task. Functions help divide a large program into smaller, understandable parts. Modular programming is the practice of organizing a program into modules with clear responsibilities and interfaces. A module may consist of one or more source files and headers.
Benefits of functions:

x: Reuse: the same operation can be called from several places.
Readability: a meaningful function name describes a task.
Testing: functions can be tested independently.
Maintenance: one implementation can be changed without rewriting every caller, as long as its interface remains stable.
Abstraction: callers need to know what a function does, not every detail of how it does it.
Teamwork: separate modules can be developed with clear interfaces.

b.x: A function should normally have one coherent responsibility. For example, calculate_average should calculate an average, while read_marks should handle input. Combining input, calculations, output, and file access into one huge function makes testing and debugging harder.
7.1 Function prototype
A function prototype declares the function’s name, return type, and parameter types before it is called:

This tells the compiler that add accepts two int arguments and returns int. The semicolon ends the declaration. A prototype allows the compiler to check calls for incompatible argument types and the number of arguments.
7.2 Function definition
The definition provides the body:

The return type is int. The parameter names a and b are local to the function. The return statement sends the computed result back to the caller. A non-void function should return an appropriate value on every path where its result is used.
7.3 Function call
A call requests execution:
The arguments 3 and 4 are passed to the function’s parameters a and b. The function calculates 7 and returns it, so result receives 7.

The prototype makes add known before main calls it. The definition may appear before main instead, in which case a separate prototype may not be needed for that call, but prototypes in headers are common in modular programs.

A function declared void does not return a value:

The void inside the parameter list means the function takes no arguments. In modern C, writing int main() is not the same declaration as int main(void) in all older language contexts; int main(void) clearly states that main takes no parameters.

sec.t: Parameters, Arguments, Scope, and Return Values
sec.s: Parameters are variables listed in a function definition or declaration.

b.x: Parameters are variables listed in a function definition or declaration. Arguments are the values supplied by a caller. In:

x: int multiply(int x, int y) { return x * y; }

b.x: x and y are parameters; 4 and 6 are arguments. Parameters have local scope inside the function body. A variable declared inside a block is generally usable only within that block, while a file-scope variable has a wider scope.

C passes arguments by value. The function receives its own parameter object initialized from the argument value. Changes to a parameter do not directly change the caller’s ordinary variable. Pointers allow a function to access an object in the caller through its address, but the pointer argument itself is still passed by value.
Example:

The parameter x is a separate int. Assigning to x changes only that local parameter. This is true even though the variable names may be identical in different functions: each function’s local variables have their own scope and lifetime.

A function can return one value directly. If several results are needed, it may use output parameters, return a structure, or update a caller-owned object through a pointer. Choose the approach that makes the interface clearest.

sec.t: Call by Value vs Pointer-based Modification
sec.s: Strictly speaking, C uses call by value, not true call by reference.

b.x: Strictly speaking, C uses call by value, not true call by reference. In a call-by-reference language, a parameter can act as another name for the caller’s object. In C, a pointer value can be passed by value; the function can then dereference that pointer to modify the object it points to. Courses often call this “call by reference using pointers,” but it is useful to remember the technical distinction.
9.1 Demonstration of value passing
The value 25 is copied into value. The function changes its local copy.
9.2 Using a pointer to modify the caller’s object

&number obtains the address of number. The pointer parameter value receives that address. *value accesses the int stored at that address, so the assignment changes number. The NULL check protects against a null pointer, though it cannot validate an arbitrary invalid non-null pointer.
9.3 Swapping two values
Calling swap(&x, &y) swaps the caller’s values. If the function instead accepted int a and int b and swapped those local parameters, the caller’s variables would remain unchanged.
9.4 Arrays as function parameters
When an array is passed to a function, the parameter is adjusted to a pointer to the first element. The function does not automatically know the array length:

x: void print_values(const int values[], size_t count) {

b.x: The const qualifier means this function promises not to modify elements through values. The count must match the accessible number of elements. Passing the length separately is a common C design pattern.

sec.s: Recursion occurs when a function calls itself, directly or indirectly, to solve a smaller version…

b.x: Recursion occurs when a function calls itself, directly or indirectly, to solve a smaller version of a problem. A recursive solution needs:

x: A base case that stops recursion.
A recursive case that moves toward the base case.
A return process that combines or forwards results.

b.x: Without a reachable base case, recursion continues until a resource limit is reached, commonly causing stack overflow. A recursive function should make progress toward the base case on every recursive path.

A function call creates an execution context for its parameters and local variables. Recursive calls create additional contexts. When a base case returns, execution unwinds to the previous call, which resumes after its recursive call and returns its own result.
10.1 Factorial
For a nonnegative integer n:
Recursive function:

x: unsigned long long factorial(unsigned int n) {

b.x: For n = 4, the calls are factorial(4), factorial(3), factorial(2), factorial(1). factorial(1) returns 1; then factorial(2) returns 2, factorial(3) returns 6, and factorial(4) returns 24.

The return type has a finite range. Factorial grows rapidly, so even unsigned long long can overflow for modest inputs. The example demonstrates recursion; production code should validate the maximum input and handle overflow explicitly.
10.2 Fibonacci sequence
A common definition is:
Naive recursive version:

x: unsigned long long fibonacci(unsigned int n) {

b.x: This is easy to understand but inefficient. It repeats many of the same subproblems. For example, calculating fibonacci(5) calculates fibonacci(3) more than once. The number of calls grows exponentially in n, so the naive version becomes slow quickly.
An iterative version:

x: unsigned long long fibonacci_iterative(unsigned int n) {
for (unsigned int i = 1; i < n; i++) {
unsigned long long next = previous + current;

b.x: This performs linear work and uses constant extra space, though the numeric result can still overflow. Another option is memoization: store each computed Fibonacci value and reuse it instead of recomputing it.
10.3 Recursion versus iteration

Recursion can be natural for trees, divide-and-conquer algorithms, and problems defined recursively. Iteration often uses less call-stack memory and can be easier to optimize for simple repetition. Neither approach is always better. Consider clarity, input size, performance, and stack limits.

sec.s: Array errors:

b.x: Array errors:

x: Using an index equal to the array length.
Confusing sizeof(array) with element count after array-to-pointer conversion.
Forgetting that a string needs a null terminator.
Copying a string into a buffer that is too small.
Passing an incorrect array length to a function.

b.x: String errors:

x: Comparing strings with == instead of strcmp.
Using strcpy or strcat without sufficient destination capacity.
Treating a string literal as writable.
Using %s with an invalid or unterminated character array.

b.x: Function errors:

x: Calling a function without a visible correct prototype.
Forgetting a return value from a non-void function.
Returning the address of a local variable.
Expecting a value parameter to modify the caller’s variable.
Confusing parameter names with caller variable names.

b.x: Recursion errors:

x: A base case that cannot be reached.
Recursive calls that do not reduce the problem.
Forgetting to combine or return recursive results.

b.x: Compile with warnings where possible:

Use small test cases first. For arrays, test the first and last valid index. For strings, test empty strings, one-character strings, maximum-length input, and strings that do not fit the buffer. For recursion, test base cases such as factorial(0), factorial(1), fibonacci(0), and fibonacci(1) before testing larger values.

sec.s: Key ideas and examples

x: 1. If int a[6] is declared, what is the last valid index?
Three int elements with values 3, 6, and 9.
3. Why is accessing a[6] invalid for int a[6]?
Valid indices are 0 through 5; a[6] is one past the end and cannot be dereferenced.
4. What is the difference between strlen(s) and sizeof s for char s[]=“cat”?
strlen is 3; sizeof s is 4 because it includes the null terminator.
5. Which header declares strlen, strcpy, strcat, and strcmp?
It guarantees a negative, zero, or positive result, not necessarily exactly -1 or 1.
7. What does a function prototype provide?
The function’s name, return type, and parameter types to the compiler.
8. Does changing a normal int parameter change the caller’s variable?
No. C passes the argument value; the parameter is a separate object.
9. How can a function change a caller’s int?
Pass the address with &, accept an int pointer, and assign through *.
10. What two parts must a recursive function have?
A base case and a recursive case that progresses toward it.
11. Why is naive recursive Fibonacci slow?
It recomputes the same subproblems many times.
12. Can two arrays be assigned with a = b?
No. Copy elements explicitly or use an appropriate copying strategy.

sec.t: More Detailed Array Algorithms and Reasoning
sec.s: A common array task is to count how many elements meet a rule.

b.x: 16.1 Counting values that satisfy a condition
A common array task is to count how many elements meet a rule. The counter starts at zero and increases only when the condition is true:

This is different from counting the array length. The loop visits every element, but positives changes only for positive values. A useful debugging method is to trace a small array such as {-3, 0, 2, 7, -1}. The final count should be 2. Make sure the code's definition of positive excludes zero.
16.2 Copying an array
Since arrays cannot be assigned as whole objects, copy elements explicitly:

The destination must contain at least n elements. If the arrays overlap in memory, the direction of copying may matter. For raw byte copying, memcpy requires non-overlapping regions; memmove supports overlapping regions. Both are declared in <string.h>, but they copy bytes, not semantic objects with custom ownership rules. When copying arrays of simple numeric elements, element-wise assignment is clear and type-aware.
16.3 Inserting into an array
An insertion at index position shifts elements to the right to make room. The destination array must have spare capacity:

x: for (size_t i = length; i > position; i--) {

b.x: The preconditions are important: position must be at most length, and length must be less than capacity. The loop counts downward so that each element is moved before its source location is overwritten. A forward loop would overwrite values needed later.
16.4 Deleting from an array
To remove an element at position, shift later elements one place left:

x: for (size_t i = position; i + 1 < length; i++) {

b.x: The final old element remains physically in the allocated buffer, but it is outside the logical length and should not be treated as part of the array's current data. This distinction between capacity and logical length is common in dynamic-array implementations.
16.5 Sorting concept
Sorting arranges elements in ascending or descending order. A simple bubble sort repeatedly compares adjacent elements and swaps them when they are in the wrong order:

x: for (size_t j = 0; j + 1 < n - pass; j++) {

b.x: This version illustrates the idea, but it assumes n is handled carefully: if n is zero, expressions involving n - pass can underflow when size_t is unsigned. A production version should explicitly handle n < 2 and use conditions that cannot underflow. Bubble sort has O(n^2) worst-case time and is not the preferred algorithm for large arrays; it is useful pedagogically because the comparisons and swaps are easy to trace.

sec.t: More String Practice and Safe Buffer Design
sec.s: A string has a current length and its character array has a capacity.

b.x: 17.1 Length versus capacity

A string has a current length and its character array has a capacity. For char name[30], capacity is 30 bytes, but the current string may be much shorter. At most 29 ordinary characters can be stored as a valid string because one byte is needed for '\\0'. The buffer capacity must not be confused with strlen(name).
17.2 Manually counting a string

This loop demonstrates how strlen works conceptually. It is safe only if text points to a valid null-terminated string. If no terminator occurs in accessible memory, the loop reads beyond the object. The standard library function is usually preferable, but understanding the loop clarifies why the terminator matters.
17.3 Manual string copy

This demonstrates copying character by character. It is only safe if destination is large enough for all source characters plus the terminator. A manual loop does not automatically become safer than strcpy; safety comes from knowing and checking capacities.
17.4 Manual comparison

This simplified comparison assumes both inputs are valid strings. Standard strcmp has more precise ordering behavior and should be used when lexical ordering is needed. Equality-only comparisons can also be implemented with a loop, but library functions are well-tested and communicate intent.
17.5 Removing a newline from fgets input
fgets may retain a newline at the end of the buffer. One common technique is:

strcspn is declared in <string.h>. It returns the number of initial characters in line that are not in the string "\\n". If a newline exists, the expression replaces it with a terminator; if none exists, it writes the terminator over the existing terminator. This assumes line is already a valid null-terminated buffer, as it will be after successful fgets.
17.6 Why string copying is a security topic

Buffer overflows occur when a program writes beyond the capacity of an array. An overflow can corrupt nearby data, crash a program, or create a security vulnerability. The root cause is often a mismatch between data length and destination capacity. Safe design includes tracking the capacity, limiting input, checking lengths before concatenation, and reporting inputs that are too long rather than silently truncating them when truncation would change the meaning.

sec.s: A small program can be organized into three layers: input/output, processing, and data…

b.x: A small program can be organized into three layers: input/output, processing, and data representation. For example, a marks program may have one function to read marks, one to calculate the average, one to choose a grade, and one to display the report. Each function can then be tested independently.
A prototype is often placed in a header file:
The implementation can live in math_utils.c:

A separate main.c includes the header and calls add. The source files are compiled and linked together. This separation helps prevent accidental mismatches between callers and definitions. The header provides the public interface; the .c file provides the implementation.

Avoid defining ordinary non-static global objects in a header included by many source files, because that can create multiple-definition errors. Headers usually contain declarations, type definitions, macros, and carefully chosen inline definitions. A function declared static at file scope has internal linkage, meaning it is usable only within that translation unit. The word static has other meanings in other contexts, so interpret it based on where it appears.
Function design checklist:

x: Choose a name that describes the task.
Select a return type that represents success, failure, or the result.
Decide whether parameters are inputs, outputs, or both.
Use const when the function should not modify an object through a pointer.
Validate sizes and pointers at the boundary.
Avoid a function doing many unrelated jobs.
Test ordinary values, boundaries, and error conditions.

sec.s: For recursive code, draw a call trace.

b.x: For recursive code, draw a call trace. For factorial(4), the calls descend: factorial(4) needs factorial(3); factorial(3) needs factorial(2); factorial(2) needs factorial(1); factorial(1) returns 1. The return values then travel upward: 2 × 1 = 2, 3 × 2 = 6, 4 × 6 = 24. This downward and upward movement is the central idea of recursion.

A recursive function can be correct but still unsuitable for large inputs. Every call consumes some execution resources. Deep recursion can exhaust the call stack. Tail recursion is a form where the recursive call is the final operation, but standard C does not require compilers to optimize tail calls. Do not rely on tail-call optimization for correctness.

Fibonacci shows the difference between a recursive definition and an efficient algorithm. The naive function matches the mathematical recurrence but repeats work. Memoization stores previously computed results. Iteration keeps only the previous two values and updates them in a loop. For many numeric sequences, dynamic programming turns a clear but slow recursive definition into an efficient implementation.
Recursive thinking is useful beyond arithmetic:

x: Visiting nodes in a binary tree.
Solving problems that naturally split into smaller similar problems.

b.x: Before writing recursion, answer: What is the smallest valid input? What does the function return for it? How does each call reduce the problem? How are the returned values combined? What is the maximum practical depth? If these questions do not have clear answers, the recursive design is incomplete.

sec.t: Extra Practice: Arrays, Strings, Functions, Recursion
sec.s: Given int a[8], what are the valid indexes?

x: Given int a[8], what are the valid indexes? Answer: 0 through 7.
If char s[] = "BCA", what is sizeof s on a system with 8-bit char? Answer: 4 bytes: three letters plus '\\0'.
Why can strlen fail on an unterminated char array? Answer: It keeps reading until it finds a null character, possibly outside the array's valid memory.
What is the difference between strcpy and strcat? Answer: strcpy copies a string into a destination; strcat appends a string to the end of an existing destination string.
How should strcmp be tested for equality? Answer: strcmp(a, b) == 0.
Why is a function prototype useful? Answer: It lets the compiler check calls against the declared parameter and return types before the function definition is encountered.
What happens when a function changes an int parameter? Answer: Only the local parameter changes; the caller's variable is unchanged.
How can a function swap caller variables? Answer: Pass their addresses and swap the values through pointer parameters.
What is a recursion base case? Answer: A case that returns without making another recursive call.
Why is factorial(0) defined as 1? Answer: It is the mathematical convention that makes factorial identities and combinatorial formulas work consistently.
What is the time complexity of naive recursive Fibonacci? Answer: Exponential growth in the input index; repeated subproblems cause a rapidly increasing number of calls.

Can a C array be returned directly from a function? Answer: No, not as an array value. A function can return a pointer, return a structure containing data, or fill caller-provided storage. Returning a pointer to a local automatic array is invalid.

b.x: For arrays, know declaration, initialization, zero-based indexing, traversal, searching, aggregation, and bounds. Understand row-major layout for 2D arrays and why a 2D array parameter needs its column dimension.
For strings, know that a valid C string ends in '\\0'. Distinguish length from capacity. Understand what strlen, strcpy, strcat, and strcmp do, and why destination buffers must be large enough.

For functions, distinguish prototype, definition, and call. Know the role of parameters, arguments, return values, and scope. Remember that C passes arguments by value; pointer parameters can provide controlled access to caller-owned objects.
For recursion, trace calls through a base case and back through return values. Compare recursive and iterative solutions, and watch for stack depth, time complexity, and numeric overflow.
The best practice method is to write small programs, predict outputs before running them, use compiler warnings, test boundary cases, and explain each line in your own words.

b.x: The example highlights several design decisions. The array is passed as a pointer-like parameter, so each function receives the element count separately. The const qualifier expresses that the functions inspect marks but do not modify them. The average uses a cast before division so that integer division does not discard the fractional part. highest_mark assumes n is greater than zero, so a general-purpose function should either reject empty input or return a separate status that communicates failure.

The total is an int, which is sufficient for this small sample. For arbitrary input sizes or large values, choose a type whose range safely covers the maximum possible sum and check for overflow where necessary. The function count_passes returns size_t because it represents a count, and %zu is used to print that type.

sec.t: Mini Project: String Validation and Comparison
sec.s: Suppose a program asks a user to enter a short command.

b.x: Suppose a program asks a user to enter a short command. A bounded input buffer avoids writing beyond the array. The program can remove the newline, then compare the string against recognized commands.

The buffer stores at most 31 input characters plus a null terminator. If the user enters a longer line, fgets reads only the first portion; a robust interactive program should detect whether the newline was captured and discard or process the remaining input deliberately. The strcmp comparisons are case-sensitive: "Start" does not equal "start". If case-insensitive matching is required, choose a portable strategy or a documented implementation-specific function.

This design demonstrates why strings are not compared with ==. The command array expression usually converts to a pointer, so == would compare pointer values rather than the text contents. strcmp examines the characters and returns zero for equal strings.

sec.s: When revising arrays, draw the indexes and values in a table.

b.x: When revising arrays, draw the indexes and values in a table. For a[5], write index 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 explicitly. Then trace each loop iteration. This habit helps identify off-by-one errors before the program runs.

When revising strings, draw every character including the terminating '\\0'. For "cat", the array initialized from the literal has four elements: 'c', 'a', 't', '\\0'. Compare the capacity of the buffer with the number of visible characters. Remember that a valid string requires space for the terminator.

When revising functions, label the prototype, definition, and call separately. A prototype announces the interface, a definition supplies the body, and a call requests execution. Follow the argument values into local parameters and track the returned result back to the caller.

When revising call by value, draw two separate variables: the caller's number and the function's parameter copy. Then repeat the diagram with a pointer parameter: the pointer value is copied, but dereferencing it reaches the caller's object. This distinction prevents the common misconception that C has a special call-by-reference parameter mechanism.

When revising recursion, make a trace table with columns for the function argument, recursive call, and returned value. Start from the base case and work upward. For Fibonacci, list F(0) through F(6) and notice that the naive recursive tree recomputes earlier terms. This naturally motivates iteration and memoization.

Finally, compile and run every example. Predict the output before running it, then explain any difference. Use warnings and test boundary cases. Understanding why a program works is more valuable than memorizing a single output.

sec.t: Additional Function and Array Edge Cases
sec.s: An array parameter does not preserve the original array length automatically.

b.x: An array parameter does not preserve the original array length automatically. For example, this function's parameter is effectively a pointer:

The number 100 in this parameter declaration does not force every caller to pass an array with 100 elements, and inside the function sizeof data gives the size of a pointer rather than 100 times sizeof(int). Pass a length parameter and validate it against the caller's actual storage.

When using size_t for indexes, remember that it is unsigned. A loop written as "for (size_t i = n - 1; i >= 0; i--)" does not stop as expected because i >= 0 is always true for an unsigned value. If n is zero, n - 1 underflows immediately. A safer reverse traversal can use:
This visits indexes n - 1 down to zero and also handles n equal to zero without entering the body.

Functions should make preconditions explicit. A function that returns the maximum array element needs a nonempty array. A function that calculates an average needs a nonzero count. A string function needs a valid terminated string. If those requirements may not hold, design an error result, status return, or output parameter so the caller can handle failure instead of letting the function access invalid memory.

A function that returns a pointer must also document how long the pointed-to object remains valid. Returning a pointer to a static array may keep the storage alive, but repeated calls can overwrite the same array and it is not automatically thread-safe. Returning a dynamically allocated pointer can work, but the caller must know it owns the memory and must release it. Returning a pointer to a caller-provided buffer can be useful when the caller controls capacity.
